hook: The last queen of ancient Egypt, who outwitted Rome for twenty years.

pages.x: Cleopatra VII was born in 69 BC into the Greek family that had ruled Egypt since Alexander the Great. Sharp and well educated, she spoke many languages, and was the first of her family to learn Egyptian. At 18 she became queen alongside her younger brother.

Pushed out by her brother's advisers, she wanted to meet Julius Caesar, who had arrived in Alexandria. Plutarch says she was carried into the palace rolled up in a bedding sack. Caesar was charmed. He put her back on the throne, and she had his son, Caesarion.

She ruled Egypt for 21 years and kept it independent while Rome swallowed its neighbours. She ran its grain trade, rebuilt its fleet, and was worshipped by Egyptians as the goddess Isis. On temple walls she appears as a pharaoh; on her coins, as a Greek queen.

The Roman writer Pliny tells a famous story. Cleopatra bet Antony that she could spend a fortune on a single dinner. She took off one of her enormous pearl earrings, dropped it into a cup of vinegar, waited for it to dissolve and drank it. It is probably only a legend.

With Mark Antony she had three children and ruled the eastern Mediterranean. Octavian called her a foreign witch who had bewitched a Roman general, and Rome declared war on her. After their defeat at Actium in 31 BC, they fell back to Alexandria.

With Antony dead and Octavian holding her prisoner, she refused to be paraded through Rome in chains. In August 30 BC she died at 39, perhaps from the bite of an asp, an Egyptian cobra, smuggled to her in a basket of figs. Egypt became a Roman province.

Cleopatra was the last ruler of independent ancient Egypt, a shrewd queen who for two decades used Rome's greatest men to protect her kingdom. Her enemies wrote her story, but she was above all a brilliant politician.
pts: The last queen of independent ancient Egypt
Kept Egypt free of Rome for 21 years
Allied with Caesar and Antony, two of the most powerful men alive
